html:
This section zooms in on "reasoning", explaining the nature of reasoning/S2 processes then describing how it is reliant on lower- and middle-order skills being mastered/stabilized and how it is directly derived from previous capabilities on the level of hardware/systems-level architecture

Reasoning likely evolved to produce arguments to convince others and to evaluate the arguments of others.

Increasing efficiency/compression allows one to hold more variables in their fixed-size mental workspace, allowing increasing abstraction; the brain cannot reach higher levels of reasoning until lower-level primitives are compressed enough to run in the background without consuming the mental workspace (Robbie Case)

cognitive development is not "modules switch on," but network reconfiguration: circuits become specialized through histories of co-activation, pruning, and changing connectivity patterns

Psychology of planning

Motivation and Volition in the Course of Action

Abstract Concepts and the Embodied Mind: Rethinking Grounded Cognition

Abstract concepts are systematically structured by metaphorical mappings from embodied domains [Lakoff]

System 1 is an "ocean" of latent patterns. Ungrounded generation is an "unbaited cast" yielding priors. Reasoning is "baiting" (context/goals) and "filtering" (constraints) to catch specific, rare outputs. Hallucinations, lack of planning, etc are reframed as coordination failures 4.

Tenenbaum et al. (2011) argue that Bayesian models are best suited to explaining "those inductive computations that the mind performs well" (p. 1280). These are rapid, reliable, unconscious processes of the kind identified within dual system theories as System 1 processing. Connectionist models, in turn, are typically invoked as neurological accounts of System 1 processes. Some limitations of Bayesian models also suggest that they capture largely System 1 processing. Bayesian models do not establish what hypotheses are relevant to consider in the first place. Although the theorem revises one’s degree of belief in a hypothesis, it does not allow one to conclude with any certainty whether a hypothesis is true, acceptable, or sufficiently supported. Also, the theorem cannot model the process of modification or revision of a hypothesis. These are all processes that are likely to be System 2 in origin.

Probabilistic program induction that is gradually meta-learned via meta-RL accumulated over the years

Monte Carlo sampling of a hypothesis space can approximate the ideal solution produced by Bayes’ theorem without having to test more than one hypothesis at a time and without having to test all relevant hypotheses 5. Supercharged by priors on the hypothesis space, which are accessible via analogy or first-principles reasoning.

Where does goal-directed planning fit into this?

Reasoning as the strategic parameterization, initiation, and evaluation of simulations (of varying levels of abstraction and varying degrees of explicitly logical content)

Learning to reason is learning a library of parameterizations and triggers. Over development you don’t just get better simulators; you acquire reusable "reasoning modes": reductio, case-splitting, counterexample search, causal graph tinkering, thought experiments, etc. The reflective system learns when to deploy which mode and how aggressively. That’s part of why adult reasoning can look propositional in some contexts: we’ve trained up a handful of logic-like parameterizations that specialize in abstract, symbol-heavy domains.

So cognitive development is essentially a sequence of stages where the next level of abstraction is mastered (which corresponds to pruning of the next set of brain regions, which corresponds to the next set of brain regions having sufficiently low predictive coding errors across time such that their wiring is much more "burnt in" for efficiency’s, continual learning’s, and development’s sake). The brain naturally moves onto the next tier of abstraction as it runs out of things to learn at the current tier.

The more abstract, the less context-/ content-specific the representation

Reasoning about possibilities: Modal logics, possible worlds, and mental models; New Paradigms in the Psychology of Reasoning; Cognitive Foundations for Reasoning and Their Manifestation in LLMs; Reasoning Across Minds and Machines

Markovitz appears to have an interesting perspective (dual strategies of reasoning: counterexample and statistical) 10

Dual process models

The brain defaults to fast, domain-specific, heavily learned processes (System 1) and recruits slower, capacity-limited, strategically controlled processes (System 2) when goals, stakes, or novelty justify the cost. Both systems operate over structured representations that can sometimes be expressed in propositional form, and System 2 in particular can deploy fragments of propositional logic when the task and training support it (especially for abstract, decontextualized content). However, most everyday reasoning is probabilistic, heuristic, and simulation-based rather than a clean implementation of classical propositional logic. System 1 does quick, shallow models (often one model) guided by heuristics; System 2 forces you to consider alternative models, counterexamples, and edge cases, but it’s costly and capacity-limited.

Barrouillet (2011) maintains that construction of the initial or default model on conditional reasoning problems is a System 1 process, whereas the fleshing out of additional models, as appropriate, and their manipulation in working memory, is an analytic or System 2 procedure-that is, one that is controlled, intentional, effortful, and constrained by working memory capacity.

Fundamental nature of reasoning

Synthesis: there is no single "format" of reasoning. The brain defaults to fast, domain-specific, heavily learned processes (System 1) and recruits slower, capacity-limited, strategically controlled simulations of varying abstraction (System 2) when goals, stakes, or novelty justify the cost. Both systems operate over structured representations that can sometimes be expressed in propositional form, and System 2 in particular can deploy fragments of propositional logic when the task and training support it (especially for the most abstract, decontextualized content). However, most everyday reasoning is probabilistic, heuristic, and simulation-based rather than a clean implementation of classical propositional logic; the brain’s core "currency" for reasoning is model-based simulation with rule-like operations over those models, and classical logic is a special-purpose toolkit learned on top of that, not the native language of thought.

The ability to reason logically with abstract premises ("If P then Q") appears only during early adulthood (Markovits and Lortie-Forgues, 2011, Markovits and Vachon, 1990, Venet and Markovits, 2001)

Probablistic accounts argue that human reasoning it closer to approximate statistical inference than strict logic

Beliefs are graded; "p implies q" is really something like "in most worlds compatible with my knowledge, if p is true then q is also true"; P(q|p)

Reasoning often looks like Monte Carlo sampling: you draw a few candidate possibilities from your implicit generative model and approximate probabilities from those samples. Heuristics and biases then fall out of limited sampling, wrong priors, or resource constraints, not from "irrational" logic.

System 1 is then something like "fast approximate inference from cached priors and heavily learned mappings," and System 2 is "controlled manipulation of priors, queries, and sampling strategies" (e.g., deliberately searching for counterexamples, trying to debias your own estimates, or recomputing rather than taking the cached answer).

Markovitz appears to have an interesting perspective (dual strategies of reasoning: counterexample and statistical) 10

Mental model theory fundamentally asserts that reasoning is not the application of formal logical rules (syntax) to abstract symbols. Instead, it posits that reasoning is semantic and simulation-based. This is likely more representative of what’s actually happening during reasoning (especially for concrete problems, which are easiest to simulate) and how reasoning arises (i.e reasoning arises from everyday simulations, not internalization of propositional logic), but propositional logic may nonetheless serve as a useful model of human reasoning (mental models often resemble propositional logic + propositional logic is genuinely approximated in its fully abstract form, but reasoning does not arise from the approximation of propositional logic); the result is clearly (and necessarily) probabilistic in nature, however.

The times when actual propositional logic is applied (instead of strategic simulation) actually may more-so reflect a "system 1" capability; after simulating "raining →\to wet" 1,000 times, it stops running the full physics simulation and just creates a shortcut vector in a higher-order latent space. For more unfamiliar or complex problems, however, we need to carefully parameterize simulations, compute and cache their results, and accumulate evidence for potential conclusions. In this case, there may be logical operations at play, but the process is better described as strategic simulation.

The Nature of Reasoning: Strategic Execution of Parameterized Simulations

Mental model theory fundamentally asserts that reasoning is not the application of formal logical rules (syntax) to abstract symbols. Instead, it posits that reasoning is semantic and simulation-based.

Parameterized Simulations: The theory defines a "mental model" as an iconic representation. This means the structure of the model corresponds to the structure of the situation it represents (like a diagram or a 3D engine).

Objects and Relationships: You are correct that these models are parameterized by objects (entities, tokens) and the relationships (spatial, temporal, causal) between them.

Kinematic Models: In dynamic reasoning, these models are "run" in time (simulated) to predict outcomes, effectively acting as a physics engine or "world model" in the brain.

Strategic Execution: Reasoning is viewed as a "strategic" process because humans do not have infinite working memory. We cannot simulate every possibility. Therefore, we use heuristics and strategies to decide which models to build and which counterexamples to search for. The "execution" is the manipulation of these models in working memory to check for consistency.

This representation then opens onto a conceptual space consisting of three distinct classes of objects or events (Markovits, 2004; Markovits & Barrouillet, 2002). One class consists of possibilities that are complementary to the conditional. These are cases where something other than p is combined with the denial of q (e.g., it is a clear day and the street is dry). A second class comprises alternatives to the antecedent. These are cases involving objects or events that are different from p and where q is affirmed (e.g., the street is being cleaned and the street is wet). In other words, these are alternative ways in which q is realized. The third class comprising this conceptual space consists of disablers of the conditional in the major premise. Disablers represent conditions (e.g., the street is covered with a tarp) that, when paired with p, render the conditional false. Disablers qualify the applicability of the conditional and must be suppressed or bracketed in order for the rule to hold.

If you try to synthesize these, a pretty plausible modern view is:

The core machinery is a generative, structured world model that supports simulation. Content can be concrete (objects, actions, people) or abstract (numbers, sets, truth values, causes, policies).

System 1 consists of very fast ways of querying this model: pattern-completion, recognition, overlearned policies, heuristics that map cues to actions or judgments. This includes "single-shot" simulations and highly cached results (e.g., "don’t touch the stove coil; it burns").

System 2 is a control system that can:

Inhibit default moves and force additional sampling or model building.

Change the query (e.g., "what would have to be true for this argument to fail?").

Enforce abstract constraints (like logical consistency, cost-benefit criteria, or epistemic norms: "consider the base rate," "consider the opposite," "check alternative hypotheses").

Recruit explicit symbolic tools (logic, algebra, graph-like dependency structures) when the person has learned them.

Within this frame, the three "big" theories become:

Mental logic: A description of some of the explicit, symbolic "mindware" System 2 can deploy, especially in math/logic-like contexts.

Mental models: A description of the representational format for the simulations and how errors arise when models are underspecified.

Probabilistic theories: A description of how beliefs and uncertainties are updated when you query those models under resource limits.

Logic is a specialized skill that lives inside and atop a broader simulation architecture; you don’t get human-like reasoning by starting with pure logic and bolting on heuristics, you get it by starting with simulations and then learning explicit logical schemas as tools for certain kinds of problems.

Analogical reasoning is core; we map new things onto existing relational structures (especially in HPC, mPFC, and rlPFC)

A detailed look at the development of specific logical constructs reveals a pattern of purely intuitive or implicit understandings preceding more explicit understanding.

More evidence that children’s understanding of logical necessity proceeds from implicit to explicit involves findings that while 7-year-olds recognize that logical truths are true everywhere and will never change, they do not appreciate that logical truths cannot be imagined to be different and are distinct from social conventions and physical laws in this and other respects. This latter, more explicit understanding is absent for several additional years (Komatsu & Galotti, 1986; Miller, 1986; Miller et al., 2000). Thus a fully explicit or formal understanding of logical necessity may be a relatively late development. This seems to parallel findings for closely related logical constructs such as logical indeterminacy and falsification, both of which are sufficiently explicit by 8 or 9 years of age to be evident in children’s performance on concrete problem-solving tasks but are not yet evident in performance on deductive-reasoning paradigms.

Children’s understanding of inference also proceeds from being relatively implicit to being relatively explicit. The beginnings of an explicit understanding of inference are evident around 6 years of age. It is at this time that children display a basic, but reasonably explicit, appreciation that inference can be a source of knowledge and the basis for beliefs (Pillow, 1999; Sodian & Wimmer, 1987), and that premise information is important to inference (Rai & Mitchell, 2006). Six-year-olds also attribute greater certainty to deductive inference than to guessing with regard to their own cognitive activity (Pillow, 2002). At the same time, much of the young child’s knowledge of inference remains implicit. Six-year-olds do not clearly appreciate when there is sufficient information present for inference and when not (Miller, Hardin, & Montgomery, 2003), and distinguishing between deduction and guessing with respect to another person’s thinking may not be present until 8 to 9 years (Pillow, Hill, Boyce, & Stein, 2000). Interestingly, it is also at this age (8 to 10 years) that children begin to make consistent distinctions between their own inductive inferences and guesses (Pillow & Pearson, 2009), while failing to achieve the same degree of consistency in their judgments about the inductions and guesses of another person (Pillow & Pearson, 2012). Attributing greater certainty to deductive inference than to inductive inference, even with respect to the child’s own thinking, is also absent until about 8 to 10 years (Galotti, Komatsu, & Volez, 1997; Pillow, 2002), particularly for stronger forms of induction (Pillow & Pearson, 2009). Even 10-year-olds are not convinced that deductive inference allows for no alternative outcomes, whereas inference about the nature of an ambiguous object does (Pillow, 2012). A full appreciation of the deductive-inductive distinction in inference forms appears to emerge during adolescence with the first indications of an explicit awareness that inferential validity is a function of argument form and independent of the truth and falsehood of the premises (Markovits et al., 1989; A. K. Morris & Sloutsky, 1998; Moshman & Franks, 1986; Venet & Markovits, 2001; but see A. K. Morris, 2000, for evidence of training effects in preadolescents). Similarly, prior to preadolescence, children do not use inference as a category with which to organize cognitive processes or types of thinking, and they do not see it as constructive in nature (Amsterlaw, 2006).

Going from sensorimotor to concrete operational

Going from preoperational to concrete operational

How is this modeled; how does it happen

System 2 (also prefrontal cortex) can be divided into two classes (Stanovich)?:

Intelligence vs rationality; define them cognitively, behaviorally, and anatomically

Under Stanovich’s framework, intelligence provides the model of the world; your rationality is the accumulation of "epistemic value" (learning what is true about yourself) and "instrumental value" (learning how to achieve your goals)

Both are present early on but are unconscious

Young children (as early as infancy) apply EVC, implicitly understanding that agents choose goals and actions to maximize the rewards they expect to obtain relative to the costs they expect to incur 11 and, in their own actions, increasing deployment of control when rewards are higher 12

Infants will imitate adult behavior only when this makes sense in relation to a given goal (Gergely et al. 2002); they learn and reason in statistical and inferential ways (Teglas et al. 2011, Xu & Kushnir 2013), rationally infer causes of failed actions (Gweon & Schulz 2011), and assume that others select goals and actions to maximize rewards relative to their incurred costs according to a naive utility calculus (Jara-Ettinger et al. 2016). Strikingly, infants also rationally infer the value of goals from the costs of actions (Liu et al. 2017), suggesting that the computational machinery for an EVC is present already very early in development. Further, it has been shown that infants apply this knowledge to their own actions and decide when and how to deploy effort (Lucca et al. 2020), whereby infants varied systematically and rationally in whether, when, and how hard they tried based on the type of social evidence and their own ongoing experience with a task.

Because these components are separate, they can be completely out of sync. Stanovich coined the term "Dysrationalia" to describe the state of having high intelligence (Algorithmic) but low rationality (Reflective). This explains why a genius PhD candidate might join a cult or fall for a Ponzi scheme. Their Lateral PFC (Intelligence) is fully capable of rationalizing the bad decision with complex logic, but their Medial PFC (Rationality) failed to detect that the goal itself was inconsistent with reality.

The algorithmic subsystem is construed as a system of rules that mirror forms of logical arguments. The reflective subsystem contains epistemic and metalogical norms along with thinking dispositions and metacognitive processes.

Algorithmic component (intelligence)

This is your World Model. It learns the dynamics of the environment (P(st+1|st,at)P(s_{t+1} | s_t, a_t)). It represents the state space.

The efficiency of your brain’s processing power. It covers working memory, logical computing, and the ability to run complex simulations.

knowledge bases, procedures, strategies, rules, and other cognitive structures underlying norm-based processing of reasoning and decision-making problems (Stanovich et al., 2012)); the mindware that supports rational thought

Intelligence is mostly about cognitive capacity and efficiency. It’s descriptive: "How good is this system at solving these problem classes?"

Functions

Decoupling, pattern recognition, and simulation

Decoupling (holding a hypothetical in mind), working memory, and executing complex rules or strategies.

This is the measure of raw computational power and efficiency. It is the ability to maintain decoupled representations in working memory (WM) and manipulate them without interference.

This is the seat of "Cold" Executive Function. It handles working memory, logical manipulation, planning, and abstract reasoning. It is the "scratchpad" where you run the cognitive simulations Stanovich talks about. Maps onto lateral PFC.

Handles the computational load. If this is damaged, you literally "cannot" solve the problem.

Metrics

Measured by Fluid Intelligence (Gf) or IQ tests.

"Do I have the raw processing power to solve this complex graph?"

Failure modes

Dementia/Dysexecutive Syndrome: "I can’t figure out the puzzle."

Reflective/intentional component (rationality)

This is the Policy/Actor and the Critic. It holds the "personality" (the reward function and constraints) and uses the World Model to select actions that align with the "Self."

Can be divided into instrumental/goal-based and epistemic/understanding-based rationality

This is the control structure that dictates which computations the intelligence engine should run. It involves epistemic rationality (holding beliefs that map to the real world) and instrumental rationality (optimizing behavior to achieve goals). This involves the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) and the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), which integrate the "cold" calculations of the DLPFC with "hot" value signals (emotional markers, past rewards, sense of self).

The control structure that decides when to use that processing power. It covers goal prioritization, epistemic self-regulation (caring if your beliefs are true), and the "override" mechanism that stops you from doing something stupid but easy.

Conceptions of self/personality/values/behavior that can guide decision making. A "self" is essentially a unified utility function. Without a stable conception of self (personality/values), an agent cannot have consistent long-term goals. It might solve a math problem brilliantly one minute (Intelligence) and then delete its own operating system the next because it lacked a value hierarchy (Irrationality).

practical and epistemic forms of self-regulation that embody, respectively, two primary forms of rationality-instrumental or goal-based rationality and epistemic or understanding-based rationality.

Rationality is normative: we can say "this belief is miscalibrated relative to the evidence" or "this decision is dominated in expected value by an alternative."

Functions

Goal management, epistemic regulation (caring if things are true), and "override detection" (noticing when you need to stop and think).

This is the seat of "Hot" Executive Function. It integrates emotions, social norms, valuation (is this good or bad?), and goal hierarchies. It connects the "thinking" brain to the "feeling" body (limbic system). Maps onto medial/ventral PFC.

Handles the valuation. If this is damaged, you can solve the problem, but you won’t-you will act on impulse instead.

Notices conflicts ("this feels wrong").

Actively checks for bias.

Decouples imagination from reality ("what if I’m wrong?", "what else could explain this?").

Chooses to deploy slow, effortful reasoning when it matters.

careful Bayesian updating, robust self-critique, explicit uncertainty handling, strong consistency checks

Metric

Measured by Thinking Dispositions (e.g., Need for Cognition, Actively Open-Minded Thinking).

"Do I value the truth enough to pause and check if my gut feeling is wrong?"

Failure modes

Acquired Sociopathy: "I can solve the puzzle, but I’ll gamble away the prize money."

Overarching models of human reasoning

Categorization is "Baked" Into the Brain

See "Conclusions Regarding the Development of Deductive Reasoning" section for overview of each theory’s support 14

Mental logic theories

posit that the logical rules governing operations within classic or standard symbolic logic are an idealization of the rules underlying mature human thought

What mental logic theory is really claiming is not "the brain literally runs full propositional calculus," but that people have an internal repertoire of inference schemas (if-then, and-elimination, modus ponens, etc.) that operate over something like sentence-level representations. On that view, a chunk of PFC (plus language areas) is implementing rule-like transformations over structured propositions. That seems broadly compatible with what we know: lateral PFC is good at holding discrete relations in working memory, binding roles and fillers, and applying task rules. So "PFC approximates propositional logic" is a decent shorthand if you remember it means "implements a small library of rule-like operations over structured representations," not "contains a mini theorem prover."

Mental models theories

Argue that we don’t use logical rules at all. Instead, we build spatial, semantic simulations of the world (models) in our heads and accept a premise if it holds under all simulations.

Verdict

Competence is almost never deployed over bare propositions. It’s almost always operating over mental models / simulations: structured situation representations with objects, relations, causality, space, time. When you "apply logic" in real life, you’re usually doing something like: construct or fetch a partial world-model; highlight a few propositions that summarize important constraints; then run rule-like operations over those within the model, not in a vacuum. So the "logic module" is more like a set of transformation operators on a simulation than a free-floating axiomatic engine. The contents of these simulations range from concrete, perceptual scenes to highly abstract relational structures, depending on task demands.

Even when System 2 intelligence could in principle follow a clean logical derivation, it usually doesn’t: it shortcuts with heuristics, uses partial models, and leans heavily on background knowledge. Belief bias, content effects, "valid but unbelievable" vs "invalid but believable" syllogisms all make sense if you assume that logic is just one constraint among many-competing with priors, goals, and working-memory limits-rather than the master representation everything is forced into.

PFC implements a library of abstract control programs, some of which approximate logical rules over structured representations, and many of which don’t look especially logical at all.

With all of that being said, propositional logic can still serve as a useful model for the move from concrete to abstract thinking

Deduction, induction, and propositional logic

Propositional logic is "content-free" and only cares about the form of the argument; deductive claims are verified against the rules of propositional logic. Propositional logic is (one way or another) implemented in compressive "reasoning schemas"

Induction is fundamentally different

Capable of generating new knowledge/theories from observations

Deduction offers certainties while induction offers probabilities

Propositional logic actually flags inductive reasoning as invalid; for example, the inductive pattern "If P then Q; I observe Q; therefore P" is formally the logical fallacy of affirming the consequent. Yet, this is exactly how scientific and machine learning models work-we observe data (Q) and infer the model parameters (P).

We use inductive reasoning to learn the rules of the world, essentially generating the premises. Once those premises are established via induction, we switch to deductive reasoning (often formalizable by propositional logic) to make predictions or plan actions based on that model.

Going from Concrete to Formal Operations

How is this modeled; how does it happen

Class logic and propositional logic are both useful; define each of them cognitively, behaviorally, and neurally

PFC operates over abstract, decontextualized representations, performs multi-step transformations on them (logical, relational, counterfactual), uses controlled simulation, and strategically caches partial results to reduce future compute

Expanding the scope of the negation operator

Think of bounded negation as "not-X within some active frame," and unbounded negation as "NOT(P)" where P is an arbitrary proposition.

Bounded negations "signify" because they still refer to something positive (a subclass) and they "delimit" because they carve out structured boundaries within a known class (e.g saying "not a rose" and "is a flower"). They are precursors to full propositional negation but not yet the abstract, free-floating operator found in formal logic (e.g saying "not a flower"). The negation of a Class A (e.g., roses) within a hierarchical classificatory system is bounded because it is equivalent to the affirmation of the complementary class (A′ ; other flowers) under the nearest superordinate (B; flowers). Full, unbounded, or nonsignifying negation (e.g., all nonflowers) cannot be directly represented within the groupings, though it can be approximated by expanding the reference frame for negation beyond the immediate superordinate (e.g., by abstracting from the class of flowers to the class of plants; Müller et al., 1999).

A lot of experience with class logic leads to the understanding of the *relatively* unbounded negation (relatively because the space of concepts remains ultimately bounded); the PFC learns a higher-order pattern over class logic regions and elaborates on it, leading to generalized, relatively unbounded operators

Imagine you’re at the grocery store looking for something to drink. You’re standing in front of a wall of beverages, and you think: "I want something that’s not soda." Here your negation is clearly bounded. You are implicitly affirming the domain "drinks in front of me" and carving out the subregion that excludes soda. You’re still operating over perceptual and semantic manifolds: tea, juice, flavored water, etc. This is bounded negation: it affirms the domain and delimits a subset within it. You’re not running a truth-functional operator over a proposition; you’re filtering a category.

Contrast that with you reading a health article that says, "All sodas are harmless." You respond internally, "That’s not true." Now you’re not picking a subset of drinks. You’re negating the proposition "All sodas are harmless." You might still drink soda later; your mental operation is about the truth status of a general statement. That’s unbounded negation: NOT(P), independent of any particular sensory context.

In short: whenever the negation feels like "filtering within a concrete set I’m currently working over," it’s bounded. Whenever it feels like "declaring some general claim or pattern ’not true’ (or some combination of claims ’can’t be true together’)," you’re firmly in unbounded, PFC-style operator territory.

Class logic is less expressive? Expressivity as degree of recursiveness?

Class logic in the ventral stream

A bounded negation like "not-rose," "not-red," or "not-dog" doesn’t require an abstract, truth-functional NOT. It only requires representing a complement inside a known category. That kind of operation can be implemented by any system with:

a structured feature space,

an existing category boundary, and

the ability to carve out a sub-region.

That is almost exactly how the ventral visual stream behaves: objects and categories are encoded as manifolds, and "not X" corresponds to suppressing the X manifold and activating nearby or alternative manifolds. Nothing here requires a symbolic operator; it’s just reshaping activity inside a representational landscape.

Unbounded negation requires a free-floating operator detached from any specific domain. Unbounded negation-Piaget’s "true" operator-is something like:

NOT(P) regardless of what P is about.

NOT applies to propositions, hypotheses, counterfactuals, and even abstract statements with no perceptual content.

That requires the brain to represent:

a domain-general operator,

that applies equally across content,

over variables that stand in for arbitrary propositions.

That is precisely the kind of content-independent control computation that shows up in the lateral PFC, especially:

rostrolateral PFC (abstract rule manipulation, variable binding),

mid-dorsolateral PFC (relational integration),

inferior frontal regions (logical operators, linguistic scaffolding).

This machinery supports the brain’s late-developing ability to detach operations from the content they manipulate-the signature of formal reasoning.

Propositional logic in PFC as predictive coding (and abstraction) over class logic systems

The PFC isn’t inventing logic out of nowhere; it’s discovering the algorithmic invariants embedded in lower-level representational systems.

Because the PFC learns the pattern across domains-rather than any single domain-its emerging operators become:

domain-general (apply equally to objects, relations, events, propositions),

variable-based (operate over placeholders rather than specific content),

unbounded (not tied to perceptual features or class hierarchies),

truth-functional (manipulate propositions beyond class membership).

The operator "NOT" becomes something like:

a rule that reverses the value of an arbitrary proposition, not merely the selection of a complement inside a semantic map.

Similarly, "IF-THEN" becomes:

a dependency relation that generalizes across any domain, not just "roses are flowers."

In this view, PFC formal logic is a learned abstraction over class logic

So the development of reasoning in humans can be modeled as a transition from a reliance on sets (clustering) and operations between sets to being able to generate propositions and perform operations on them

Moving from class logic (logic applied to groupings and classifications of real objects) to propositional logic (logic applied to statements, hypotheses, and abstract variables). They no longer need physical objects to perform logic; they can perform logic on the propositions describing those objects. They can evaluate the logical validity of a statement like "If PP, then QQ" regardless of whether PP and QQ are factual.

Propositional logic (PFC) and class logic (ventral/dorsal stream) appear to contiunually coexist and have their niches. Propositional logic can be directly derived from class logic, which explains how propositional logic arises in the brain (PFC predictive coding over ventral/dorsal streams; via uncinate fasciculus and superior longitudinal colliculus) and why its symbols are grounded.

Class logic keeps reasoning coupled to the structure of the immediate environment-to specific sets, categories, and their inclusion relations. "Not-P" still means "the rest of this category structure," and the child’s inference space is anchored to concrete hierarchies (roses -> flowers -> plants -> things). Logical operations are still tied to what things are out there. Propositional logic emerges when logical operations-especially negation-are no longer defined by the world’s category structure but by formal manipulation of truth values. "Not-p" becomes a symbolic operator you can apply to anything, regardless of whether it corresponds to a real category or even a possible state of the world.

"One potential advantage of the Piagetian propositional logic as a competence model is that it can be derived from a more fundamental logic of classes and relations, and as such, it comprises part of a theoretically viable account of the emergence of deductive reasoning from earlier, more limited, logical competencies. In fact, Piaget’s logical competence model is unique in this regard. The derivation of Piaget’s propositional logic involves, in part, an expansion of the scope of negation in the class and relational logics (Byrnes, 1988; Byrnes & Overton, 1988; Müller et al., 1999; Piaget, 2001), and the emergence of formal deductive competence from an earlier, concrete competence can be represented as a process of increasing fl exibility in the use of partial or local negations leading to the differentiation and coordination of two forms of negation-one bounded and the other unbounded (Byrnes, 1988; Piaget, 1980, pp. 297-299; Piaget & Garcia, 1991, p. 164). This theoretical claim has been supported empirically. Müller et al. (1999) provide evidence that the a priori ordering of logic problems in terms of their complexity with regard to the role of negation corresponds to a developmental progression." 15

when the authors say propositional logic can be "derived from a more fundamental logic of classes and relations," they mean: if a child already understands how to manipulate classes, complements, and relational orderings at the concrete level, then you can lift those same operations to operate over sets of possible states, which yields the propositional calculus.

you don’t build a "logic engine" separate from the "physics engine." The logic engine is just the physics engine refactored to operate on symbols instead of sensory inputs. You cannot program a "true" understanding of logic into an agent by just giving it a truth table. According to Piaget, the agent must first experience the physics of containment and separation. The "logic" is just the optimization of those physical physics engine calls.

Potential stages

V0 (Transductive): Simple associations

V1 (Concrete): Build an agent that can classify and sort entities (Class Logic) and understand Partial Negation (identifying the complement of a set).

V2 (Transition): Introduce problems where Partial Negation fails (e.g., where the set is open-ended).

V3 (Formal): The agent abstracts the negation operator to apply to the relationship between states, enabling Propositional Logic.

Why Class Logic is "More Fundamental"

Class logic (the logic of sets, groupings, and categorization) is considered the primitive foundation because it operates directly on perceptual reality.

Tangibility: It requires only the ability to perceive similarities between objects (e.g., "These are all red things"). Propositional logic requires the ability to manipulate abstract statements that may not exist in front of you.

Part-Whole Architecture: It is built on the nested structure of physical matter. A "motor" is physically part of a "robot."

Understanding this physical inclusion (A⊂BA \subset B) precedes understanding the abstract implication ("If motor, then robot").

Computational Cost: Class logic requires a single mental step: Membership Check (x∈Ax \in A). Propositional logic requires a meta-step: evaluating the Truth Value of that membership (True/FalseTrue/False).

class operations can be "lifted" from concrete sets of objects to abstract sets of possibilities (possible states of the world)

Piagetian theory argues that logical connectives are just internalized versions (i.e versions that are decoupled from physical reality) of physical sorting actions.

Conjunction (AND) = set intersection (e.g finding objects that belong to both pile A and pile B.)

Disjunction (OR) = set union (e.g combining pile A and pile B into one larger heap.)

Negation (NOT) = set complement (e.g Identifying everything left over outside of pile A.)

Implication (if/then) = set inclusion (e.g Recognizing that object X is entirely contained inside pile B.)

Inner and Outer Loops: Enrichment versus Conceptual Change

AGI Application: Your architecture needs two distinct optimization loops.

Inner Loop: Gradient descent/Hebbian updates (Enrichment).

Outer Loop: Symbolic Program Induction (Conceptual Change). You cannot reach AGI solely by "enriching" a pre-training loss curve; the agent must periodically "refactor" its internal code to support higher abstractions.

In this view, the brain is an engine that searches the space of computer programs (generative models) to find the one that best explains the data, using "Core Knowledge" as the library of primitive functions.

the key lesson is: a world model is a theory-like structure; realistic learning systems must sometimes perform structural updates on their representational schemes, not just tweak weights on fixed features.

Scientific reasoning

The prefrontal cortex is the principle *abstract* hypothesis generator, and its roles in "working memory", "cognitive flexibility", "inhibition", and "planning" (the 4 classic executive functions) simply reflect the most abstract section of the world model:

"Working memory" reflects the need to strategically activate, maintain, and integrate across distributed representations (whether they’re semantic, episodic, procedural, emotional, gustatory, etc) when making abstract judgments (e.g "I tripped someone yesterday on purpose" (episodic/procedural) + "Getting tripped hurts" (procedural/emotional) + "I tasted blood and felt pain last time I was tripped" (gustatory/emotional/episodic) + "Jimmy is mean and he tripped someone too" (semantic/episodic) -> query each into working memory (perhaps sequentially) and let attractors settle -> "I am mean" (abstract representation (self schema) represented as a PFC firing pattern, which is directly connected to the evidence/items fed into working memory while making this judgment)); shows up both when learning a new abstraction and when reactivating an existing abstraction (although rules can likely be pulled into working memory without the original associated lines of evidence/items also being activated [])

"Cognitive flexibility" reflects the need to switch between abstractions according to external and internal states (including according to other abstractions)

"Inhibition" reflects the causal influence of active abstractions (abstractions are in "working memory" and are rhythmically suppressing other regions)

"Planning" reflects the PFC’s responsibility to maintain and and enforce abstractions that guide internal simulations such that the PFC can derive motor abstractions that will lead to desired world states. Emergence of longer INTs and relation to abstract representations

Mechanistically, longer INTs in transmodal cortex don’t arise because neurons would "die" unless they encode higher-order features; they arise from circuit and network design. Association areas show stronger local recurrence, denser long-range feedback, and sit at the crossroads of white-matter highways (connector hubs/rich club), all of which lengthen integration windows and promote context accumulation. Large-scale dynamical models that incorporate inter-areal heterogeneity and measured connectivity reproduce a hierarchical spread of timescales purely from these architectural differences. At the microcircuit level, slower synaptic kinetics (notably NMDA-receptor dominated recurrent excitation) and E/I balance favor persistent/reverberatory activity, which extends timescales and enables maintenance of abstract, task-relevant state.

There is also a developmental story that makes abstraction more likely-but again by biasing learning, not an existential "survival test." Association cortex matures late, myelinates slowly, and retains protracted plasticity. That extended window, plus convergence of diverse inputs, lets these regions fit higher-order, cross-modal, temporally extended structure in the world; neurons that wire into these long-range motifs get activity-dependent stabilization, while less informative synapses are pruned. That picture is consistent with the observation that intrinsic dynamics covary with microstructural and gene-expression gradients across cortex.
